c01.question: A support agent calls lookup_order with the same order number over and over until the iteration limit fires. What is most likely broken?
options: The tool description is too short, so the model does not realise it already ran
Tool results are not appended to the message history, so the model sees identical context every time
The iteration limit is too low — it should be raised to 30
Temperature is set too high and the model makes random decisions
c01.explanation: The model keeps no state between calls: it only sees the history you send. If the assistant response containing the tool_use block and the following tool_result are not appended to messages, every iteration starts from the same context and produces the same decision.

c01.question: Which signal correctly drives continuation of an agentic loop?
options: A marker word ("done", "DONE") appearing in the response text
The type of the first content block: text means completion
The stop_reason field: continue while it equals "tool_use"
The iteration counter: exit once the maximum is reached
c01.explanation: stop_reason is the one explicit protocol field. "tool_use" means the model requested tools and is waiting for results; "end_turn" means it is finished. The other three infer protocol state from prose or from an external counter.

c01.question: If stop_reason determines termination, why does a correct agentic loop still need MAX_ITERATIONS?
options: It is the primary stopping mechanism: without it the agent never terminates
It is a safety net against an unbounded loop; hitting it is an anomaly worth logging as an incident and escalating
It saves tokens and should fire on most runs
It caps how many tools the model may call within a single iteration
c01.explanation: The cap protects against pathological behaviour (a failing tool, a loop), but should not fire in normal operation. If it fires regularly the system is shipping half-finished answers — the correct reaction to exhausting the cap is an error and escalation, not returning whatever text is at hand.

c01.question: The model returns a response with two blocks: text ("Let me check your order") and tool_use (lookup_order). What should the loop do?
options: Treat the work as complete, since the response contains a text block
Execute the tool, return a tool_result with the same tool_use_id, and continue the loop
Drop the text block and skip appending the assistant response to history
Send the text to the user and start a new conversation with a clean history
c01.explanation: The model routinely talks and acts in one response, and stop_reason will be "tool_use". The assistant response goes into history in full, the tool runs, the result comes back with the same tool_use_id, and the loop continues.

c01.question: A team describes their system: "the code always calls get_customer, then lookup_order, then asks the model to phrase the reply." How should this be classified?
options: An agentic loop with model-driven decision making
A multi-agent system with a coordinator
A pre-configured workflow: the tool sequence is decided by code, not by the model
An agentic loop in which stop_reason is replaced by a step counter
c01.explanation: The defining property of an agentic loop is that the model chooses the next tool from context. A call sequence hardcoded in code is a workflow. That is perfectly appropriate where the order is mandatory — but it should not be called an agent, and it does not need a stop_reason loop.

c02.question: In a multi-agent research system the "synth" subagent cites data that appeared in no source. The logs show "docs" returned the phrase "see previous discussion". What is the cause?
options: The synth subagent ran with too high a temperature
A subagent does not inherit the coordinator history: the task arrived with no substance and the model filled the gap itself
The coordinator invoked the subagents in the wrong order
The synth system prompt does not forbid hallucination
c02.explanation: Subagent context is isolated — it only sees the task it was handed. A reference to a shared discussion is empty for it, so the model fills in the blank. The fix is a self-contained task: goal, all required data, expected format.

c02.question: Which statement is true of a hub-and-spoke architecture?
options: Subagents exchange intermediate results directly to take load off the coordinator
The coordinator is the single point through which tasks, results, errors and routing all pass
Every subagent has access to the coordinator full history
The coordinator only assembles the final answer; each subagent handles its own errors
c02.explanation: The point of hub-and-spoke is that all traffic goes through the centre. That gives one place for error handling, logging and routing decisions — and makes the system explainable.

c02.question: The coordinator always runs every request through all four subagents. Users complain that a simple factual question takes six minutes. What does the exam expect as the solution?
options: Run the four subagents in parallel instead of sequentially
Cache subagent results between requests
The coordinator should analyse the query requirements and dynamically select which subagents to invoke
Lower max_tokens on each subagent
c02.explanation: The skill tested explicitly: the coordinator analyses query complexity and requirements and invokes only the subagents that are needed, rather than always running the full pipeline. Parallelism and caching are optimisations — they do not remove the unnecessary work.

c02.question: Analysts complain that broad survey requests come back as reports with large gaps in coverage. Which decomposition risk is this?
options: Overly narrow decomposition by the coordinator — incomplete coverage of a broad topic
Too many subagents, so their results contradict each other
Overflow of the coordinator context window
Missing retries when a subagent fails
c02.explanation: The guide names this risk directly: a coordinator that can only produce pointed subqueries will return a handful of unrelated facts for a broad topic. Broad topics need a cut by dimension — players, pricing, technology, regulation.

c02.question: Which responsibility does NOT belong to the coordinator in this architecture?
options: Decomposing the request into subtasks
Aggregating subagent results into a single answer
Performing the domain work itself when a subagent returns an error
Handling subagent errors and deciding how to route next
c02.explanation: The coordinator owns decomposition, delegation, aggregation and error handling. It should not stand in for a subagent: on a failure it decides whether to retry, call someone else, return a partial result or escalate — not do the work itself.

c03.question: The coordinator is defined and configured, but in the logs it always does the work itself and never spawns a subagent. What do you check first?
options: That the subagents have system prompts defined
That the coordinator allowedTools includes "Task"
That the coordinator has a large enough max_tokens
That the subagent descriptions are under 200 characters
c03.explanation: Subagents are spawned by the Task tool. If it is missing from the coordinator allowedTools, delegation is physically impossible and the model does everything itself — with no error raised, which is what makes the symptom confusing.

c03.question: Three subagents are independent and take 90 seconds each. How do you run them in parallel?
options: Call Task one at a time in separate turns so the coordinator can react to each result
Emit several Task calls in a single coordinator response
Triple the iteration limit of the agentic loop
Give all three one shared session so they can share context
c03.explanation: One model response can carry several tool_use blocks. Several Task calls in one response is exactly what parallel subagent spawning is. Separate turns give sequential execution and triple the wait.

c03.question: In the synthesiser final report, claims lose their source citations even though the web agent found them. Which technique does the exam require?
options: Ask the synthesiser in the prompt to "remember to cite sources"
Pass findings as structured data with content and metadata (source_url, document, page) in separate fields
Lower the synthesiser temperature to zero
Forbid the synthesiser from paraphrasing prior agents
c03.explanation: A source embedded in a sentence gets lost in paraphrase. A structured format separates content from metadata, and attribution reaches the report. A prompt request helps but is not a mechanism.

c03.question: Yesterday you spent half a day debugging in Claude Code, then rewrote half the affected files in the evening. What is the right way to continue today?
options: Resume with --resume and immediately ask where you left off
Resume the session and state which files changed so the agent re-reads exactly those
Fork yesterday session to preserve the original branch
Continue without mentioning the changes: the agent will notice the mismatch on its next read
c03.explanation: Resumption is right while context is mostly valid, but the agent is reasoning from earlier file reads. It does not know about the changes until you say so — then it re-reads selectively instead of reasoning from stale data.

c03.question: The agent spent half an hour analysing a codebase and now you want to compare two refactoring strategies without repeating that analysis. What do you use?
options: fork_session — two independent branches from the shared analysis baseline
--resume twice with the same session name
Two new sessions with a structured summary of the analysis
One subagent instructed to consider both options in a single response
c03.explanation: This is what fork_session is for: the shared analysis baseline is preserved and the branches proceed independently. Resuming one session twice would tangle the two lines of reasoning, and fresh sessions would mean repeating the analysis.

c04.question: An audit found that in 9% of refunds the agent skipped identity verification, even though the system prompt demands it in capitals. What do you do?
options: Rewrite the instruction more forcefully and add few-shot examples of the correct order
Set temperature to zero so the behaviour becomes deterministic
Add a programmatic prerequisite: block process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer
Raise the iteration limit so the agent has more chances to run the check
c04.explanation: Prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate — that is a property of a probabilistic system. Where deterministic compliance is required (compliance, money, irreversible actions), ordering is enforced in code: a hook or a prerequisite gate.

c04.question: The gate blocked a process_refund call. How should that be communicated to the model?
options: Raise an exception and abort the conversation
Return a tool_result error stating which step is missing
Silently skip the call and continue the loop
Send the customer a message about a technical error
c04.explanation: The block comes back as a tool result with a clear explanation: "call get_customer first". The model sees it in the history, understands what is missing, and performs the missing step itself — the ordering holds and the conversation survives.

c04.question: A customer describes three problems in one message. What approach does the exam expect?
options: Answer the first problem and ask them to submit the others separately
Decompose into distinct items, investigate each in parallel on shared customer context, and synthesise one unified answer
Escalate to a human, since multi-concern requests are outside the agent scope
Handle the items strictly sequentially, re-fetching customer data for each
c04.explanation: The skill is stated directly: decompose a multi-concern request into distinct items, investigate each in parallel using shared context, then synthesise a unified resolution. Shared context matters — customer data is fetched once.

c04.question: What must a structured handoff summary contain when escalating to an operator?
options: The full conversation transcript, so the operator misses nothing
Customer identifier, root cause, amount, and recommended action
Only the recommended action: the operator can find the rest in the CRM
A customer satisfaction estimate and the sentiment of the conversation
c04.explanation: The summary is written for a human without access to the transcript. It therefore needs the customer id, the established root cause (not a retelling of the chat), the specifics of the operation, and the proposed action.

c04.question: In which case is a system-prompt instruction sufficient, making a programmatic gate unnecessary?
options: Identity verification before a financial operation
Never sending a customer email without human confirmation
The preferred tone of voice and message structure
The cap on an autonomous refund amount
c04.explanation: A prompt is good at style, tone and preferred ordering — the cost of deviation there is small. A gate is required where a violation costs money or compliance, or is irreversible: identity checks, refund caps, anything sent outside.

c05.question: Tools from three MCP servers return dates as a Unix timestamp, ISO 8601 and DD/MM/YY, and status as a numeric code. The agent periodically gets time wrong. What do you apply?
options: A PostToolUse hook reducing the formats to one shape before the model sees the result
A description of every format in the system prompt, with examples
A dedicated converter subagent that receives the raw results
A lower temperature on the main agent
c05.explanation: This is the guide example verbatim: PostToolUse normalises heterogeneous data from different MCP tools before the agent processes it. A prompt copes most of the time, but normalisation in code is deterministic.

c05.question: The rule "no refund above $500" must apply identically across three different agents. Where does it belong?
options: In each agent system prompt
In an outgoing call interception hook attached to all of them
In the description of the process_refund tool
In each agent loop as its own condition
c05.explanation: An interception hook is a guarantee and applies to every agent it is attached to, regardless of their prompts. A condition inside the loop has to be copied three times and will drift the first time the policy changes.

c05.question: A hook blocked a call that violates policy. How does the guide describe the correct behaviour?
options: Block and return a refusal to the model with no explanation
Block and end the conversation with an error
Block and redirect to an alternative workflow, such as human escalation
Allow the call but flag it in the logs as a policy violation
c05.explanation: The skill is phrased as "block policy-violating actions and redirect to alternative workflows". A bare refusal leaves the agent with no way forward, so it retries the same call.

c05.question: Which requirement is NOT solved by a hook and correctly stays in the system prompt?
options: Guaranteeing identity is verified before a financial operation
Turning numeric status codes into readable values
The preferred tone of voice and the structure of the customer reply
Forbidding refunds above a threshold
c05.explanation: Tone and response structure are probabilistic preferences where deviation is cheap, and a prompt suits them. Anything where a violation costs money or compliance, or is irreversible, moves into hooks and gates.

c05.question: What is the difference between a PostToolUse hook and an outgoing call interception hook?
options: PostToolUse only works with MCP tools, interception only with built-in ones
PostToolUse transforms the result after execution; interception decides the fate of the call before execution
PostToolUse runs on the model side, interception on the server side
There is no difference: they are two names for the same mechanism
c05.explanation: They are two different lifecycle positions. Outgoing call interception sits before execution and can forbid the action; PostToolUse sits after execution and changes the result before the model processes it.

c06.question: A review agent receives an 18-file diff in one request and returns comments about the first two files only. What is this called and what do you do?
options: Context window overflow — halve the size of the diff
Attention dilution — split into per-file local passes plus a separate cross-file pass
Insufficient max_tokens — raise the response limit
An overly strict system prompt — soften the finding criteria
c06.explanation: The diff fits in the window, but the more material in one request, the shallower each part is analysed. The guide recipe is a local pass per file plus a separate pass looking for cross-file inconsistencies.

c06.question: A PR changed a function signature in one file while the call site in another stayed stale. Why will per-file local passes not catch it?
options: A local pass sees one file only, and the defect exists between files — a separate cross-file pass is required
A local pass does not read function signatures
Only a static analyser finds such defects; an agent is useless here
It will catch it if the local pass prompt asks it to check dependencies
c06.explanation: A mismatch by definition does not fit inside either file. Asking for it in the local pass prompt does not help: the second file is simply not in its context. You need a separate pass working over the summaries of all files.

c06.question: The task: "get a 40,000-line legacy module under test". Which decomposition strategy is correct?
options: A fixed pipeline: walk the files alphabetically and write tests for each
Split into equal 5,000-line chunks and process them in parallel
Map the structure first, then identify high-impact areas, then build a prioritised plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered
Write tests for every public function, starting with the longest
c06.explanation: This is an open-ended task: the work is not enumerable upfront. The guide describes exactly this sequence — structure map, high-impact areas, prioritised adaptive plan. Alphabet and equal chunks ignore where the risk sits.

c06.question: When is a fixed pipeline (prompt chaining) the right choice?
options: When the list of aspects to check is known upfront and does not depend on findings
Always: it is cheaper than dynamic decomposition
When the task is open-ended and the structure is unknown
When exploring an unfamiliar codebase
c06.explanation: Prompt chaining suits a predictable multi-aspect review: the steps are known before you start and each receives the previous result. Open-ended tasks need dynamism, because their subtasks are born from intermediate findings.

c06.question: Why must a plan for an open-ended task adapt rather than be written once?
options: Because the model forgets context between steps
Because dependencies and obstacles are discovered along the way and change the priorities
Because the user may change their mind
Because a fixed plan costs more tokens
c06.explanation: The value of an adaptive plan is that subtasks are generated as findings accumulate. Once you start on one module you learn about its dependencies — and a rigid plan written before that knowledge falls apart.

c07.question: Two tools are described as "Analyzes content and returns key findings" and "Analyzes a document and returns key findings". The agent keeps picking the wrong one. What do you fix first?
options: Add a rule to the system prompt about which tool to call when
Rename the tools and rewrite the descriptions to remove the functional overlap
Merge both tools into one general-purpose tool
Set tool_choice: any so the model definitely calls a tool
c07.explanation: The description is the primary tool-selection mechanism. With overlapping descriptions the choice becomes arbitrary. The guide prescribes renaming and sharpening descriptions with an explicit boundary: how this tool differs from its neighbour.

c07.question: The analyze_document tool can extract metrics, write summaries and verify claims. What should be done with it?
options: Leave it and extend the description to list all three modes
Split it into purpose-specific tools with defined contracts: extract_data_points, summarize_content, verify_claim_against_source
Add a mode parameter with values extract, summarize, verify
Move the mode selection into the system prompt
c07.explanation: The guide describes this move directly: split a generic tool into purpose-specific tools with defined input/output contracts. One tool with three modes leaves the output contract vague and the selection harder.

c07.question: An MCP tool returned an archive access failure. Which fields let the agent make the right decision?
options: Just a human-readable error message
isError, errorCategory, isRetryable and a readable message, plus customer-facing text for business errors
The HTTP status code and the server response body
An attempt counter and the time until the next retry
c07.explanation: Structured metadata is the whole point: the category conveys the nature of the failure, isRetryable saves pointless attempts, and customerMessage lets the agent explain the reason to a human in plain language.

c07.question: An archive search ran successfully but found no matches. What should the tool return?
options: isError: true with category transient so the agent retries
isError: true with category validation, since the query produced nothing
A successful response with an empty results list
An "Operation failed" error — the agent will work it out
c07.explanation: The guide asks specifically for distinguishing access failures (which need a retry decision) from valid empty results (a successful query with no matches). Erroring on an empty result sends the agent hunting for a problem that does not exist.

c07.question: A subagent hit an external service timeout, retried, and got the data on the second attempt. What propagates to the coordinator?
options: Nothing about the error: the transient failure was resolved locally, only the result goes up
A full log of both attempts, so the coordinator knows about the instability
A transient-category error, so the coordinator can decide whether to retry
A partial result flagged as possibly incomplete
c07.explanation: The skill is phrased as local error recovery within subagents for transient failures, propagating to the coordinator only errors that cannot be resolved locally — along with partial results and what was attempted.

c08.question: All four subagents were given one shared list of 18 tools. The synthesiser started searching the web itself, and call counts on simple requests went up. What do you do?
options: Restrict each subagent set to the tools of its role, leaving 4–5 relevant ones
Improve the descriptions of all 18 tools and keep the list shared
Set tool_choice: any so the model stops hesitating
Add a list of forbidden tools to each subagent prompt
c08.explanation: A large tool count degrades selection reliability by increasing decision complexity. On top of that, an agent holding tools outside its specialisation tends to misuse them. Role scoping fixes both at once.

c08.question: You need to guarantee extract_metadata runs before the enrichment tools. How is that done?
options: tool_choice: "any" on every step
Forced selection {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} on the first call, with subsequent steps in follow-up turns
State the ordering in the enrichment tool description
Disable the other tools until metadata has been obtained
c08.explanation: Forced selection pins the first step: a specific tool is guaranteed to be called, and the following steps are processed in later turns. It sets the start of the route, not the whole route.

c08.question: A team MCP server is needed by every developer on the project and requires a token. How do you configure it?
options: Add the server to each developer ~/.claude.json with their own token
Add it to the project .mcp.json with the token in plain text — the repository is private
Add it to the project .mcp.json, expanding the token from the environment via ${VAR}
Put the token in a separate file next to .mcp.json and add that file to .gitignore
c08.explanation: The project .mcp.json describes shared team servers and is committed; secrets stay out of it thanks to environment variable expansion. The user-scoped ~/.claude.json is for personal and experimental servers.

c08.question: An MCP server with indexed code search is connected, yet the agent keeps using the built-in Grep. The most likely cause?
options: Built-in tools always take precedence over MCP tools
The MCP tool description is too thin and does not explain its capabilities or output format
The MCP server is configured at user scope instead of project scope
MCP server tools are only available after explicitly requesting a resource
c08.explanation: There is no built-in precedence — there is clarity. The guide asks you to enhance MCP tool descriptions, explaining capabilities and outputs, or the agent will prefer a clear Grep over an unclear MCP tool.

c08.question: Why do MCP resources exist when there are already tools?
options: Resources perform actions faster than tools
Resources expose a catalog of available content to the agent, reducing exploratory tool calls
Resources store the credentials used to connect to the server
Resources are only needed for servers that run over HTTP
c08.explanation: A resource answers "what is here at all": issue summaries, documentation hierarchies, database schemas. Seeing the catalog, the agent skips exploration and goes straight to the right tool.

c09.question: You need to find every place in the repository where process_refund is called. Which built-in tool is right?
options: Glob — by file name pattern
Grep — content search across files
Read — read the files and look through them
Bash — run a search command manually
c09.explanation: Grep is for content search: function names, error messages, import statements. Glob matches file paths by pattern and never sees contents at all.

c09.question: You need to find all test files matching **/*.test.tsx. What does that?
options: Grep for the string ".test.tsx"
Glob by path pattern
Read over the tests directory
Bash with a find command
c09.explanation: Glob is the file path pattern matching tool. Grep would look for mentions of that string inside files, which solves an entirely different problem.

c09.question: Edit cannot apply a change: the anchor text occurs three times in the file. What do you do?
options: Read the whole file with Read and write the modified version with Write
Repeat Edit several times — it will hit one of the occurrences
Delete the file and recreate it
Use Glob to find similar files and edit those
c09.explanation: A non-unique match means there is no unambiguous anchor, not that the file is broken. The guide names Read + Write as the reliable fallback; the alternative is widening the anchor with adjacent lines until the match is unique.

c09.question: An agent is exploring an unfamiliar codebase. Which order does the exam expect?
options: Read every file upfront to get the full picture
Start with Grep to find entry points, then Read along the imports, tracing the flows
Walk the directories with Glob and read one file from each
Ask the user for a list of important files and read only those
c09.explanation: The skill is described as building understanding incrementally: Grep finds the entry points first, then Read follows the imports. Bulk reading upfront exhausts context and yields no understanding.

c09.question: A function is re-exported from a wrapper module under a different name. How do you reliably find every caller?
options: Search the codebase for the original function name
First identify every name the function is exported under, then search for each of those names
Read every file that imports the module
Use Glob to find files with similar names
c09.explanation: Searching the original name alone misses calls that go through wrappers. The guide describes the two-step technique: collect all exported names first, then run a search for each of them.

c10.question: A new team member does not receive the testing conventions, although they work for the person who wrote them. The most likely cause?
options: The conventions are in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md — user level, which does not reach version control
The new member did not run /memory after cloning
The CLAUDE.md file is too large and gets truncated on load
Conventions must be duplicated in every subdirectory
c10.explanation: User-level settings apply only to their owner and are not shared with teammates via version control. Team standards belong in the project CLAUDE.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md in the repository.

c10.question: Test files are spread across the codebase next to their components. How do you apply shared conventions to them?
options: Create a CLAUDE.md in every directory that contains tests
A file in .claude/rules/ with frontmatter paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]
Add the conventions to the root CLAUDE.md so they always load
Use @import from every directory-level CLAUDE.md
c10.explanation: Rules with glob patterns in the paths field apply to files by type regardless of directory. The guide recommends them over directory CLAUDE.md files exactly when conventions cover files spread across the codebase.

c10.question: The root CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines and loads in full in every session. What do you do?
options: Shorten it by dropping the less important rules
Split it into topic files in .claude/rules/ and scope them with paths or wire them with @import
Move some of the rules to user level
Increase the model context window
c10.explanation: Modular organisation solves both problems: the rules become readable, and path scoping keeps irrelevant rules out of the session, saving context and tokens.

c10.question: An agent behaves inconsistently across sessions and it is unclear which instructions apply. Where do you start?
options: Clear the context and start a fresh session
Run /memory and see which memory files are loaded
Check the Claude Code version
Delete the user-level CLAUDE.md
c10.explanation: The /memory command shows the memory files actually loaded. It is the direct way to see which hierarchy levels took effect and to explain the divergence.

c10.question: In a monorepo each package has its own standards. How do you wire the relevant standards files into a package CLAUDE.md?
options: Copy the relevant sections into each package CLAUDE.md
Use @import to include only the standards files relevant to that package domain
Put every standard in the root CLAUDE.md
Create one paths rule per file in the package
c10.explanation: The @import syntax keeps CLAUDE.md modular: the package maintainer selectively includes the standards files for their domain, without copying text or loading other teams rules.

c11.question: A codebase-analysis skill produces two hundred lines of output that clutter the main session. What do you configure?
options: context: fork in the frontmatter — the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context
Add a request to be more concise to the skill body
allowed-tools restricted to Read
Invoke the skill in a separate session and copy the result over manually
c11.explanation: The context: fork option exists for exactly this: the skill runs in an isolated context and its verbose or exploratory output never reaches the main conversation.

c11.question: You need to guarantee a migration skill cannot execute commands and can only write files. How?
options: State the prohibition on executing commands in the skill body
Set allowed-tools in the frontmatter, leaving only file operations
Run the skill with context: fork
Add a rule to the project CLAUDE.md
c11.explanation: allowed-tools restricts tool access for the duration of skill execution — a guarantee at the configuration level. A prohibition in text remains a request with a non-zero failure rate.

c11.question: A changelog command must be available to every developer on the project. Where does it go?
options: ~/.claude/commands/changelog.md
.claude/commands/changelog.md in the repository
.claude/skills/changelog/SKILL.md with context: fork
Into the root CLAUDE.md as an instructions section
c11.explanation: Project-scoped slash commands live in .claude/commands/ and are shared via version control. The user scope ~/.claude/commands/ is for personal commands and is invisible to colleagues.

c11.question: You want to tune a shared review skill for yourself without breaking colleagues. The correct way?
options: Change the shared skill in the repository and warn the team
Create a personal variant in ~/.claude/skills/ under a different name
Create a personal variant in ~/.claude/skills/ with the same name so it overrides the shared one
Copy the skill into a separate repository branch
c11.explanation: Personal customisation is a variant in the user scope, and specifically under a different name: identical names make it ambiguous which skill actually ran.

c11.question: The standard "every service logs errors with structured context" must always apply. Where does it belong?
options: In a skill with an argument-hint, invoked before edits
In CLAUDE.md — it is a universal, always-loaded standard
In a slash command invoked before each commit
In the allowed-tools of every project skill
c11.explanation: The distinction is how they activate: CLAUDE.md is always-loaded universal standards, while skills and commands are on-demand invocation for a specific task. A permanently applicable rule belongs to the former.

c12.question: There is a clear stack trace: the function crashes on an empty date value, a two-line fix in a single file. What do you choose?
options: Plan mode — any change is safer when planned
Direct execution — a simple change with clear scope
Plan mode followed by direct execution
An Explore subagent for a full module analysis
c12.explanation: Direct execution suits simple, well-scoped changes: a clear cause, one file, an obvious fix. Planning here adds time without reducing risk.

c12.question: A library migration touches 45 files and there are two integration approaches with different infrastructure requirements. What do you do?
options: Direct execution: describe the task in detail and run it
Plan mode to investigate and choose the approach, then direct execution of the chosen plan
Split into 45 per-file tasks and work through them sequentially
Start with direct execution and switch to plan mode at the first problem
c12.explanation: Every plan mode signal is present: scale, many files, multiple valid approaches, architectural implications. The guide separately describes the combination: planning for investigation, direct execution for implementing the choice.

c12.question: The discovery phase of a multi-phase task produces a lot of output and risks exhausting the context. What do you apply?
options: The Explore subagent: isolate verbose discovery and return a summary to the main session
Raise the iteration limit of the main agent
Split the task across several sessions and carry the conclusions over by hand
Disable file reading and work from search alone
c12.explanation: The Explore subagent exists precisely to isolate verbose discovery output: a summary returns to the main conversation and the context window survives into implementation.

c12.question: A prose description of a transformation is interpreted differently from iteration to iteration. What works best?
options: Rewrite the description in more detail and more strictly
Give 2–3 concrete input/output examples
Lower the model temperature
Break the description into numbered steps
c12.explanation: The guide names concrete input/output examples as the most effective way to communicate an expected transformation when prose is read inconsistently. A longer description usually introduces new ambiguities.

c12.question: Four problems are found in the code: two that interact (a date format and the sorting that depends on it) and two independent ones. How do you hand them over?
options: All four in one message — it is faster
All four one at a time — it is safer
The interacting ones in a single detailed message, the independent ones sequentially
The independent ones together first, then the interacting ones one at a time
c12.explanation: The rule depends on interaction: if fixing one problem changes the conditions for another, describe them together or the work will be redone. Independent problems dumped into one message dilute attention.

c13.question: The automated review job sometimes hangs until timeout: the log shows the agent asked a clarifying question. What do you fix?
options: Raise the job timeout
Run Claude Code with the -p (--print) flag for non-interactive mode
Add a request to the prompt not to ask questions
Move the job to a self-hosted runner with a longer time limit
c13.explanation: The -p (--print) flag puts Claude Code in non-interactive mode: it performs the task and prints the result without requesting input. A prompt request leaves a non-zero chance of a question, and a longer timeout merely delays the hang.

c13.question: Review results must be posted as inline PR comments, but the free-text parser breaks whenever the wording changes. What do you apply?
options: --output-format json together with --json-schema for machine-parseable structured output
More robust regular expressions and text normalisation
A prompt request to always keep one format
A second model call to post-process the output
c13.explanation: The --output-format json and --json-schema flags produce output of a known shape suitable for automated posting. That removes prose parsing as a class of problem.

c13.question: After three consecutive commits the review posted the same findings three times. How is that fixed?
options: Run the review only on the final commit before merge
Delete the bot previous comments before each new run
Include prior findings in the context and instruct it to report only new or still-unaddressed issues
Hash the finding text and drop repeats in the posting script
c13.explanation: The guide describes exactly this: when re-running after new commits, include prior findings in context with an instruction to report only what is new or unaddressed. The model then avoids duplicating, rather than a script cleaning up after it.

c13.question: The test generator proposes getter tests and duplicates scenarios that already exist. What do you do?
options: Document testing standards, valuable test criteria and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md, and put the existing tests in context
Cap the number of proposed tests at ten
Run test generation only for new files
Lower the temperature and raise max_tokens
c13.explanation: CLAUDE.md is the mechanism for providing project context to a CI run. Documented standards and criteria cut low-value tests, and existing tests in context stop it proposing already-covered scenarios.

c13.question: Why should the review of changes not be handed to the same session that generated the code?
options: Because the context window is exhausted after generation
The session that generated the code is less effective at reviewing its own changes than an independent instance
Because the system prompt cannot be changed within one session
Because generation results cannot be passed on in a structured form
c13.explanation: This is a distinct point in the guide about session context isolation: its own decisions and justifications sit in the context and bias it toward confirming them. Review runs as an independent instance with a clean context.

c14.question: The "stale comments" category produces 87 findings, of which 4 are accepted. The prompt says "check that comments are accurate". What do you change?
options: Add "only report findings you are confident about"
Replace it with an explicit criterion: flag only when the claimed behaviour contradicts the actual code behaviour
Lower the severity of that category to minor
Cap the category at ten findings per PR
c14.explanation: The guide uses this exact pair as its canonical example: a vague instruction makes every imperfect comment a candidate, while an explicit categorical criterion demands a checkable condition — a contradiction with behaviour.

c14.question: Why does "be conservative and only report confident findings" fail to improve precision?
options: Because it conflicts with schema-enforced structured output
Because general confidence instructions fail to improve precision compared with specific categorical criteria
Because the model always ignores instructions at the end of a prompt
Because confidence must be set as a numeric threshold in the request parameters
c14.explanation: The model has no calibrated confidence threshold that a word turns down. What works is defining what counts as a problem and what to skip — categorical criteria rather than confidence filtering.

c14.question: One review category produces many false positives and developers now ignore every comment. Which skill does the guide describe?
options: Temporarily disable the problem category to restore trust while improving its prompt
Remove the category permanently as unworkable
Lower every finding in that category to minor severity
Publish that category as a separate weekly report
c14.explanation: A high false positive rate in one category undermines confidence in the accurate ones. The guide describes exactly this: temporary disabling combined with prompt improvement, not abandoning the category.

c14.question: The output format instructions are detailed, yet the result is still inconsistent from run to run. What do you apply?
options: An even more detailed instruction describing every field
2–4 targeted few-shot examples showing the desired format and the reasoning
Temperature lowered to zero
Splitting the task into two sequential calls
c14.explanation: The guide names few-shot as the most effective technique precisely when detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent results. It speaks of 2–4 targeted examples, not of covering every case.

c14.question: Why should a few-shot example show the reasoning for choosing one action over a plausible alternative?
options: To lengthen the context and increase the model attention to the task
So the model generalises judgment to novel patterns rather than matching only the enumerated cases
To make the output conform to the JSON schema
To reduce the number of tokens in the response
c14.explanation: The reasoning is what conveys the property behind the decision. Without it the example is a record of one case, and the model does not carry the judgment over to similar but new fragments.

c15.question: The document type is unknown upfront, three extraction schemas are declared, and structure must come back either way. Which tool_choice?
options: "auto"
"any"
{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_invoice"}
Leave tool_choice unset — the model will work it out
c15.explanation: The "any" mode requires the model to call a tool while letting it choose which — exactly what an unknown document type with several schemas needs. "auto" permits a text answer, and forced selection requires knowing the type in advance.

c15.question: After moving to tool use with a strict JSON schema, which errors remain?
options: None: the schema guarantees the extracted data is correct
Semantic ones: totals that do not sum, values in the wrong fields
Only JSON syntax errors
Only errors on documents longer than the context window
c15.explanation: The guide stresses this separately: strict schemas via tool use eliminate syntax errors but do not prevent semantic ones — line items that do not sum to the total, or a value placed in the wrong field.

c15.question: In 6% of cases the model returns a plausible supplier tax id that does not appear in the document. What do you change in the schema?
options: Add a prohibition on inventing values to the field description
Make the field optional (nullable) so the model is not forced to fill it
Lower the request temperature to zero
Move the field into a separate extraction tool
c15.explanation: A required field the source lacks forces the model to put something there. The skill from the guide is designing such fields as optional when source documents may not contain the information.

c15.question: A payment-terms classifier sometimes meets wording that matches no enum value. What do you provide for?
options: Extend the enum with a new value after each such case
Add an "unclear" value for ambiguous cases and the "other" + detail string pattern for extensible categories
Make the field a plain string with no enum
Return an extraction error so the document goes to manual processing
c15.explanation: Without a "cannot tell" option the model picks the nearest value and you never learn it hesitated. The guide describes both patterns: "unclear" for ambiguity and "other" plus a detail field for extensible categories.

c15.question: Dates appear in three different formats across documents. Where are the rules for normalising to YYYY-MM-DD stated?
options: In the JSON schema, via a format constraint
In the prompt, alongside the strict output schema
In post-processing after the result comes back
In the tool description field of the tool itself
c15.explanation: The schema handles types and structure, while rules for normalising inconsistent source formatting are included in the prompt alongside the strict schema — a separately named skill of this objective.

c16.question: An extraction failed validation because of a wrong date format. How do you build the retry?
options: Send the same request again, perhaps with a lower temperature
Include the source document, the failed extraction and the specific validation errors in the retry
Split the document into parts and extract fragment by fragment
Switch to another model and retry
c16.explanation: The technique is retry-with-error-feedback: the specific validation errors are appended to the prompt so the model corrects what was named. A repeat with the same prompt gives the model no new information.

c16.question: In 30% of invoices the required "contract number" field is empty, because the number exists only in a separate annex the system cannot see. What do you do?
options: Raise the extraction attempt count from three to five
Recognise that retries are ineffective: the information is absent from the source and a different document is required
Add an instruction to the prompt to look for the contract number more carefully
Lower the temperature so the model stops skipping the field
c16.explanation: The guide asks you to distinguish situations where a retry succeeds (format mismatches, structural output errors) from those where the information is simply not in the source document. In the latter, no number of retries helps.

c16.question: Invoice line items do not match the stated total and the system does not notice. Which technique does the guide describe?
options: Add a request to check the arithmetic to the prompt
Extract calculated_total alongside stated_total so the discrepancy becomes a visible field
Re-extract any invoice above a threshold amount
Validate the total with a separate model call
c16.explanation: The schema forces the model to write both values out explicitly, after which the discrepancy is checked in one line of code. That is the self-correction flow the guide describes, complemented by a conflict_detected boolean for inconsistent source data.

c16.question: Developers dismiss review findings but no pattern is visible. What do you add to the finding structure?
options: A confidence field with a numeric score
A detected_pattern field carrying a machine-readable label for the construct that triggered the finding
An author field naming the owner of the file
A timestamp field for sorting by time
c16.explanation: The skill is stated directly: detected_pattern lets you group dismissed findings by construct and analyse false positives systematically. Without the label you are left with a set of unique texts and no pattern.

c16.question: Which errors are NOT eliminated by moving to tool use with a strict schema and still require code validation?
options: JSON syntax errors
Semantic ones: values that do not sum, data in the wrong fields, contradictions in the source
Context window overflow errors
Authorisation errors when calling the tool
c16.explanation: Strict schemas via tool use eliminate syntax errors as a class, but semantics remain: that is a separate layer, closed by code validation and a retry loop carrying feedback.

c17.question: Which workload can NOT be moved to the Message Batches API for the savings?
options: Nightly test generation for changed modules
A pre-merge PR check whose result a developer is waiting on
A weekly audit of three thousand supplier documents
Building an overnight report on support tickets
c17.explanation: Batches suit non-blocking, latency-tolerant workloads: a processing window of up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee. A pre-merge check blocks a developer, so it stays on the synchronous API.

c17.question: The SLA promises results within 30 hours and batch processing takes up to 24 hours. How often do you submit batches?
options: Once a day — that is enough for a 30-hour SLA
Every 4 hours: a document must not wait more than 6 hours to be submitted, minus margin for resubmission
Every 30 hours, at the SLA boundary
Continuously, one document per batch
c17.explanation: The frequency comes from the SLA: 30 hours minus up to 24 hours of processing leaves roughly 6 hours of waiting to be submitted. Submitting every 4 hours fits that window and leaves margin for resubmitting failures.

c17.question: Some documents in a batch failed. What is the correct response?
options: Resubmit the entire batch
Resubmit only the failed documents, identified by custom_id, with the cause addressed — chunking the over-long ones, for example
Process the failed documents synchronously one by one
Halve the size of every future batch
c17.explanation: The custom_id field correlates requests with responses, which is how the failures are isolated. Resubmitting without addressing the cause reproduces the same error, and resending the whole batch doubles the bill.

c17.question: A review of generated code in the same session finds none of the problems QA later finds. What is most effective?
options: Add a thorough self-check instruction to the prompt
Enable extended thinking before the answer
Run the review as an independent instance with none of the author reasoning context
Raise max_tokens so the review is more detailed
c17.explanation: The model retains reasoning context from generation and is less likely to question its own decisions. The guide explicitly names an independent instance as more effective than self-review instructions or extended thinking.

c17.question: Why ask the model to report confidence alongside each finding in a verification pass?
options: To discard every finding below high confidence
To route review in a calibrated way: doubtful findings to a human, confident ones posted directly
To reduce the cost of the request
To make the model hallucinate less
c17.explanation: Self-reported confidence beside a finding enables calibrated routing: it decides what a human checks and what posts automatically. Simply discarding would throw away correct findings too.

c18.question: In a long conversation the agent forgot the promised refund amount and deadline: the history had been summarised. What do you do?
options: Summarise less often so details survive longer
Extract transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers, promises) into a case facts block included in every prompt outside the summarised history
Ask the model not to lose numbers when summarising
Enlarge the context window and stop summarising
c18.explanation: The progressive summarization risk is that numbers, dates and customer-stated expectations condense into vague summaries. The answer is moving them out of the summarised part into a separate case facts block.

c18.question: The model consistently misses findings from the middle of a long aggregated report. How do you mitigate that?
options: Place a key findings summary at the beginning of the input and organise details under explicit section headers
Move everything important to the very end of the input
Split the report into ten separate requests
Duplicate the middle of the report twice
c18.explanation: The "lost in the middle" effect: models reliably process the beginning and end of long inputs. The guide recommends exactly a key findings summary at the start plus explicit section headers for the details.

c18.question: Every lookup_order call returns more than forty fields, of which five are relevant. What do you do?
options: Nothing: the extra fields may come in handy later
Trim the tool output to the relevant fields before it accumulates in context
Summarise the history more often to push old calls out
Re-query the order only when needed
c18.explanation: Tool results accumulate in context and consume tokens disproportionately to their relevance. The skill from the guide is trimming verbose output to the relevant fields before it reaches the context.

c18.question: Three hours into a codebase exploration the agent stopped naming concrete classes and started answering "systems like this usually". What do you apply?
options: Raise the response max_tokens
Keep a scratchpad file of key findings and reference it, delegate verbose discovery to subagents, summarise findings between phases
Rephrase the question in more detail
Lower the temperature to zero
c18.explanation: This is the context degradation the guide describes for extended sessions. The remedies are mechanisms that survive a context boundary: scratchpad files, subagent delegation, phase summaries and /compact.

c18.question: How do you design crash recovery for a multi-agent exploration?
options: Store the full transcript of every session and reload it entirely
Each agent exports state to a known location, and on resume the coordinator loads a manifest and injects it into agent prompts
Repeat the whole exploration from scratch — it is more reliable
Keep the state in the coordinator context and never summarise it
c18.explanation: The guide describes structured agent state exports into a manifest the coordinator loads on resume. A full transcript does not fit and carries much that is irrelevant, and restarting from scratch discards hours of work.

c19.question: A customer writes: "Put me through to an agent." What should the agent do?
options: Try to resolve it first and escalate if that fails
Escalate immediately, with no attempt to investigate first
Clarify the problem so the operator gets context, then escalate
Assess the complexity and escalate only if it is genuinely complex
c19.explanation: An explicit customer request for a human is a trigger in its own right, honoured immediately. Attempting investigation first degrades the experience, as the ticket review shows.

c19.question: A customer complains angrily about delivery, but the issue is simple and a one-step replacement resolves it. What do you do?
options: Escalate: negative sentiment signals a complex case
Acknowledge the frustration and offer a resolution; escalate only if the customer reiterates asking for a human
Escalate if the model self-reported confidence is below a threshold
Reply formally and close the ticket
c19.explanation: Sentiment and self-reported confidence are named unreliable proxies for actual complexity. When the issue is within the agent capability, the right move is acknowledging the emotion and resolving it, leaving escalation for a reiterated request.

c19.question: A customer asks to match a competitor price. Policy covers price adjustments on our own site only and is silent about competitors. What should the agent do?
options: Approve the discount: not forbidden means allowed
Refuse, citing the absence of such a rule
Escalate: the policy is ambiguous or does not cover the request
Offer a compromise discount at its own discretion
c19.explanation: A policy gap or ambiguity is one of the three appropriate escalation triggers. Policy silence can be read neither as permission nor as prohibition: a human makes that call.

c19.question: A surname search returned three different customers. What should the agent do?
options: Pick the customer with the most recent order
Ask for an additional identifier: order number, email, or the last digits of the card
Handle all three cases identically
Escalate to an operator as an ambiguous case
c19.explanation: The guide requires requesting additional identifiers on multiple matches rather than selecting by heuristic. "Most recent order" is a bet whose cost lands on the customer.

c19.question: A web search subagent timed out. What should it return to the coordinator?
options: A generic status such as "search unavailable"
An empty results list, so the workflow does not break
Structured context: the failure type, what was attempted, partial results and possible alternatives
An exception that terminates the whole workflow
c19.explanation: A generic status hides valuable context from the coordinator, and returning an empty result is silent suppression — a named anti-pattern. Structured context lets the coordinator choose to retry, work around, or use the partial results.

c20.question: The system shows 97% overall accuracy. Management proposes switching off manual review. What must happen first?
options: Switch review off and watch for complaints
Analyse accuracy by each document type and each field to verify performance is consistent
Raise the confidence threshold to 0.99 for all documents
Increase the sample size on which the 97% was measured
c20.explanation: An aggregate metric may mask poor performance on specific document types and fields. The guide requires verifying accuracy by segment before reducing human review.

c20.question: Why keep sampling extractions the model marked as confident?
options: To train operators on easy examples
Stratified random sampling measures the real error rate in the automated stream and detects novel error patterns
To satisfy formal audit requirements
To stop the model overfitting to confident cases
c20.explanation: Confident extractions are sampled precisely to measure the real error rate and detect new patterns: when a document template changes, confident extractions start erring and sampling is the only way to notice.

c20.question: At what level should the model report confidence, and how are thresholds set?
options: At document level, with one threshold for all types
At field level, with thresholds calibrated using labeled validation sets
At batch level, with the threshold set by the business
Confidence is unnecessary: schema validation is enough
c20.explanation: An extraction can be confident in one field and unsure in another, so the score is needed per field. Thresholds are calibrated on labeled sets, or "high confidence" corresponds to no measured error rate.

c20.question: Two credible sources give different market size figures. What do you do in synthesis?
options: Take the value from the more authoritative source
Average the values
Annotate the conflict with source attribution, keep both values, and leave the decision to the coordinator
Drop the metric from the report as unreliable
c20.explanation: The guide requires annotating conflicting statistics with attribution rather than arbitrarily selecting a value. Analysis completes with both values explicitly annotated, and reconciliation is the coordinator decision before synthesis.

c20.question: Why must subagents include publication or data collection dates in structured outputs?
options: To make the report look more professional
So a temporal difference is not misinterpreted as a contradiction between sources
To comply with source licensing requirements
So the coordinator can sort findings chronologically
c20.explanation: Without dates, values from different periods look like a conflict when they describe a trend. The guide explicitly requires publication or collection dates for correct temporal interpretation.
